Artesunate Derivatives as Anticancer Agents: Hybrid Designs and Emerging Therapeutic Strategies.

Artesunate is a semisynthetic derivative of the natural product artemisinin, isolated from Artemisia annua and characterized by the biologically important endoperoxide bridge. Beyond its established use in malaria treatment, in recent decades, artesunate has attracted growing research interest as an anticancer agent. Despite encouraging preclinical results, clinical studies demonstrated only modest efficacy when artesunate was used as a single compound, due to its low bioavailability, toxicity, and unfavorable side effects. For this reason, artesunate derivatization has attracted significant attention, as the resulting derivatives often exhibit superior anticancer activity in both in vitro and in vivo studies compared with artesunate alone. This review offers a comprehensive overview of reported artesunate derivatives, structured into sections based on the type of molecule employed for derivatization and highlights the expanding research on their anticancer activity. Currently emerging strategies that include hybridization and nanocarrier-based delivery systems which may accelerate the clinical translation of artesunate derivatives and harness their potential in anticancer drug discovery are also discussed. While significant progress has been made, a lot of the research field still remains underexplored.

Advancing the Alzheimer's disease research and care pipeline with agentic artificial intelligence: Opportunities, challenges, and priorities from the international clinical trials on Alzheimer's disease (CTAD) task force.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) holds unprecedented potential to transform the entire Alzheimer's Disease and related dementias (ADRD) research and care continuum. During the 2025 Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease (CTAD) conference, the CTAD Task Force reviewed recent advances in the field, highlighting the emerging role of agentic AI, and discussed priorities to guide future AI-driven innovation in ADRD. Agentic AI co-scientists are emerging as transformative tools to accelerate scientific discovery by autonomously integrating multimodal data, generating and evaluating new hypotheses, and connecting previously siloed knowledge into actionable insights. Operationalized through end-to-end translational pipelines, such platforms can also link mechanistic insights to therapeutic design by automating molecular docking and drug repurposing. Complementary initiatives are creating digital wet labs for in silico experimentation. At the same time, agentic AI is increasingly being used to address pre-discovery bottlenecks by automating data harmonization and inferring missing information through digital twins and synthetic data. AI is also reshaping next-generation ADRD clinical trials, through automated assessment of clinical outcomes, precision participant stratification, individualized disease trajectory modeling and prediction of treatment response. These approaches could substantially improve trial efficiency through responder enrichment. Importantly, AI applications are expanding beyond discovery and clinical trials to support diagnosis, care navigation, and personalized disease management. To translate the momentum surrounding AI innovation into meaningful and sustainable impact across the ADRD continuum, the Task Force identified priorities including the development of AI-ready ecosystems, closer collaboration between clinicians, researchers and computer scientists, AI-enabled optimization of clinical trials and robust ethical and governance frameworks for responsible AI adoption.

Repurposing drugs for aortic aneurysm: unlocking new therapeutic opportunities.

Aortic aneurysm (AA) is a life-threatening vascular disease for which no pharmacological therapy has been proven to effectively limit disease progression. Drug repurposing (DR), which leverages existing drugs with established safety profiles, offers a promising and cost-effective strategy to accelerate therapeutic development for AA. In this review, we summarize recent advances in DR research for AA, highlighting the emerging framework that integrates computational prediction with experimental and clinical validation. We discuss key repurposed drug candidates, evaluate the current state of translational evidence, and examine the challenges that have hindered clinical success despite encouraging preclinical findings. Finally, we outline opportunities to enhance target identification, patient stratification, and clinical trial design. By bridging mechanistic discovery and translational application, DR may provide a practical pathway toward effective medical therapies for aneurysmal disease.

metadata.text:
Subunit-exchanged heterodimers reveal symmetric ATP binding and hydrolysis requirements for Escherichia coli DNA mismatch repair protein MutL clamp cycling.

DNA mismatch repair (MMR) is an evolutionarily conserved pathway that maintains genome stability by identifying and correcting replication errors. The principal proteins involved are MutS, which recognizes mismatches and MutL, which forms a ternary complex with MutS and DNA and coordinates subsequent repair reactions. Escherichia coli MutL is a homodimer comprising an N-terminal domain (NTD) with a GHKL-ATPase joined via a flexible, non-conserved linker to the C-terminal dimerization domain (CTD). Upon ATP binding, the two NTDs interact by converting MutL into a closed, stable sliding clamp on DNA. Utilizing fluorophore-labeled single-cysteine variants, we demonstrate that MutL forms dimers with sub-nanomolar affinity, which undergo slow subunit exchange in solution. We exploit this dynamic property to generate MutL heterodimers, enabling the real-time monitoring of nucleotide-driven conformational changes. Using heterodimers containing one ATPase-deficient subunit we demonstrate that MutL closure requires ATP-binding to both subunits. This ATP-binding dependent closed state can be trapped by preventing ATP-hydrolysis. Moreover, preventing ATP-hydrolysis in one subunit is sufficient to stabilize the closed state. These findings provide new mechanistic insight into how ATP binding and hydrolysis are coordinated within the MutL.

Synthon-based strategies in virtual screening of ultralarge chemical spaces: from library design to drug discovery.

Ultralarge make-on-demand chemical libraries have transformed early drug discovery by providing access to billions or even trillions of synthetically accessible compounds, which contain novel and diverse scaffolds. However, the expansion of the chemical universe also creates major computational challenges: exhaustive enumeration, storage, and conventional screening of these spaces are becoming impractical, especially as library sizes continue to grow. This has motivated the development of new computational strategies capable of navigating reaction-defined chemical spaces without explicitly generating every possible product. Among these strategies, synthon-based approaches provide an attractive balance between chemical-space exploration, computational efficiency, and synthetic accessibility. Instead of treating virtual libraries as fully enumerated compound collections, these methods exploit their underlying combinatorial organization, representing chemical spaces through building blocks (BBs), reaction rules, and synthons. This compact representation enables the development of non-enumerative workflows for ligand-based and structure-based virtual screening. In the present review, we discuss the conceptual basis of synthons in the search of novel hits in drug discovery and their relationship with BBs and make-on-demand chemical spaces. We also highlight representative applications in which synthon-based workflows have enabled the identification of novel scaffolds, active hit candidates, and optimized analogues. Finally, we also discuss the challenges to be faced in the future development of synthon-based strategies, highlighting possible insights for future studies.

Finally, we also discuss the challenges to be faced in the future development of synthon-based strategies, highlighting possible insights for future studies.

Recent Developments in Sulfonafmide-Based Anti-Malarial Agents: Structure-Activity Relationships and Future Perspectives.

Despite tremendous advancements in prevention and treatment, malaria continues to be one of the deadliest infectious illnesses in the world and a persistent public health concern. The critical need to find new chemotherapeutic drugs with better efficacy, selectivity, and resistance profiles is highlighted by the widespread rise of resistance to traditional anti-malarial drugs. Due to their exceptional structural adaptability, advantageous pharmacokinetic characteristics, and capacity to modulate several biological targets involved in the Plasmodium life cycle, sulfonamide-based compounds have garnered significant attention in anti-malarial drug discovery among the various classes of bioactive molecules. Many derivatives with strong action against drug-sensitive and multidrug-resistant strains of Plasmodium falciparum have been produced via structural modifications of the sulfonamide pharmacophore. All things considered, this review offers insightful information about the medicinal chemistry of sulfonamide derivatives and a strategic framework for the logical development of novel anti-malarial treatments.

Understanding Nonreacting Substrate Analogs as Potential Scaffolds for Inhibitor Design Against Mycobacterium tuberculosis Cystathionine β-Synthase.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis cystathionine beta-synthase (MtbCBS), a pyridoxal-5'-phosphate (PLP)-dependent enzyme, regulates sulfur metabolism and redox homeostasis, making it a model enzyme for inhibition studies and to understand scaffold behavior. Amino acids remains as an attractive scaffold for designing novel inhibitors having reduced cytotoxicity and improved properties for cellular uptake. This study integrates computational, biophysical, and structural approaches to provide for a potential scaffold that could be further modified to inhibit MtbCBS. Structure-based sequence alignment of CBS homologs identified seven conserved polar/charged regions critical for PLP-substrate interactions. Molecular docking of polar substrate analogs (threonine, histidine, glutamic acid, and arginine) at the conserved active site revealed distinct binding modes for histidine, glutamic acid, and arginine. Molecular dynamics simulations demonstrated persistent binding of histidine, stabilized by hydrophobic interactions relative to other analogs. Experimental studies revealed histidine's ability to form stable external aldimine adducts, modulating enzyme thermostability (ΔT<sub>m</sub>), akin to known reacting substrates. Finally, cryo-EM-based structural studies revealed two classes of MtbCBS, one with extra density suggesting the noncovalently bound histidine and the unbound WT MtbCBS maintaining internal aldimine. This suggests that exploration of the chemical modification space of the histidine moiety might provide us with a potential inhibitor against MtbCBS and enzymes of the RTS pathway.

Assessment of quantum mechanics-based hydropathic descriptors to navigate the isofunctional chemical space in scaffold hopping.

Scaffold hopping is a well-established paradigm in modern drug discovery, providing valuable support in the hit-to-lead and lead optimization stages due to the impact in (i) improving the activity via the exploration of structure-activity relationships, (ii) circumventing intellectual property restrictions, and (iii) optimizing the pharmacokinetics profile of drug-like candidates. The effectiveness of this approach, however, critically depends on the quality of the parameters used to describe chemical scaffolds, as appropriate filtering and prioritization can be decisive for the success of scaffold hopping. In this context, quantum mechanical (QM)-based methods have demonstrated superior performance in capturing the physicochemical features of small molecules, making them a robust complementary option for 3D similarity analyses and virtual screenings. Here we evaluated the suitability of the QM-based hydropathic (HyPhar) descriptors derived from continuum solvation calculations for scaffold hopping and navigating the isofunctional fragment space. To this end, a representative subset of real-case scaffold-hopping examples, which was assembled from the 'large-hops' (LH) benchmark dataset, was used to validate our methodology. The results showed that the HyPhar descriptors performed well in the identification of the active scaffold, outperforming the behavior observed for classical 2D and 3D molecular representations. In addition, these descriptors were also used to examine the ability to discriminate active scaffolds from decoys exploiting the hydropathicity-guided alignment for five distinct targets taken among the LH benchmark, mimicking the scenario faced in drug discovery studies. Notably, a higher early enrichment was obtained relative to docking-based computations, thus demonstrating superior capability in discriminating active scaffolds from decoys. In particularly, we proposed the use of HyPhar descriptors to rescore the poses of docked scaffolds due to the overall improvement in the prioritization of the isofunctional fragments relative to the discrimination obtained from docking calculations.Scientific ContributionTime-efficient and accurate in silico approaches are critical for the success of drug discovery programs. Here, we demonstrate that QM-MST HyPhar descriptors could provide a rapid and effective strategy for filtering and prioritizing isofunctional scaffolds in scaffold hopping. Notably, the results indicate better performances compared to other commonly used 2D, 3D scoring metrics and machine learning-based chemogenomic methods.
